newsitem.title: USA: Robust U.S. economy helps lift dollar.
newsitem.headline: Robust U.S. economy helps lift dollar.

text.p: The dollar moved higher against most major currencies Wednesday on a report of surprisingly strong first-quarter economic growth and growing worries about the British elections.
The dollar rallied to session highs after the Commerce Department reported the economy grew at a 5.6 percent rate in the first quarter, its fastest clip in more than nine years.
The news sent investors rushing to buy dollars after weak inflation data on Tuesday sent the currency tumbling for the first time in nearly a week.
It also prompted another rally in the stock and bond markets, with the Dow Jones industrials index jumping 46.96 points to 7,008.99, its first close above 7,000 since March 12.

"The upward bias in the dollar comes from low rates of inflation as measured by yesterday's number and high rates of growth as measured by today's Gross Domestic Product figure," said John Nelson, foreign exchange trading manager at ABN-AMRO Bank in New York.
Expectations for higher interest rates and a vibrant U.S. economy have pushed the dollar up 12 percent against the German mark and nearly 10 percent vs. the Japanese yen so far this year.
The dollar fell just shy of its 56-month high of 127.16 yen reached on April 10, hitting a high of 127.14 before settling at 127.05 in late New York trading, up from 126.93 yen late on Tuesday.
Meanwhile, the dollar rose as high as 1.7348 marks but backed off to end at 1.7315, up from 1.7245 at Tuesday's close.

The British pound fell to $1.6235 from $1.6323 on Tuesday as nervousness swept through the markets regarding the outcome of Thursday's general election, which according to polls will bring 18 years of unbroken Conservative Party rule to an end in favour of Tony Blair's Labour Party.
"The sterling sales are fairly aggressive and mainly in response to concerns about the election," said Mike Malpede, senior foreign exchange analyst at Refco Group Ltd.
"The polls indicate that the Labour party will win, but if the polls are wrong and the majority is slim, that argues for a paralysis in Labour government," he added.
However, the pound was in part supported by a drop in the Irish pound, which fell to its lowest level against the British pound since July 1992.
The punt succumbed to strong selling pressure on rumours that the Irish central bank stopped supporting the punt late on Tuesday after heavy intervention earlier this week.
Traders said selling pressures have mounted in anticipation of Ireland's perceived desire to enter Europe's drive for a single currency at a rate well below current market rates.
In other trading, the dollar rose to 1.4735 Swiss francs from 1.4680 and inched lower to Canadian $1.3976 from C$1.3978.
